correctness.rationale: With \(c_n=1\) for even \(n\) and \(c_n=\cos(\pi/n)\) for odd \(n\), set \(C_n=4c_n-1\) and \(h=C_n1_U-1_{2U}\). The decomposition used in the package is exact: the pointwise nonnegative measure \(\sigma=(6c_n-4)(\delta_1+\delta_{-1})\) has nonnegative coefficient because \(n\ge5\), and the remainder \(	au=h-\sigma\) has Fourier transform \(4(1-x_k)(x_k+c_n)\), where \(x_k=\cos(2\pi k/n)\). The smallest sampled cosine is \(-c_n\), so \(	au\) is of positive type. Pairing an admissible nonnegative positive-definite \(f\) with \(\sigma\) and \(	au\) proves the upper bound. The explicit witness \(f_*(j)=(c_n+\cos(2\pi\lfloor n/2floor j/n))/(1+c_n)\) has nonnegative Fourier coefficients and is pointwise nonnegative; it vanishes at the two neighbors and takes value \(2c_n-1\) at distance two, attaining \(C_n\). This gives three on even cycles and \(4\cos(\pi/n)-1\) on odd cycles. The verifier checks the primal and dual formulas through \(n=400\), but the closed dual certificate proves every \(n\ge5\).

Their full primary text develops the abstract cone duality and variants of the extremal problem but does not state the nearest-neighbor finite-cycle parity formula. The audited result is an explicit primal/dual solution of one natural finite-group instance; the general dual theorem provides the framework but not the optimal coefficient.
